```python
from collections import Counter

def perplexity(token_logprobs):                 # natural log probs of the true tokens
    return math.exp(-sum(token_logprobs) / len(token_logprobs))

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):                         # unbiased estimator (Chen et al. 2021)
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - math.comb(n - c, k) / math.comb(n, k)

def token_f1(pred, ref):
    p, r = pred.lower().split(), ref.lower().split()
    common = sum((Counter(p) & Counter(r)).values())
    if common == 0:
        return 0.0
    prec, rec = common / len(p), common / len(r)
    return 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)

print(perplexity([math.log(0.5)] * 4))          # 2.0: as unsure as a fair coin
print(round(pass_at_k(n=10, c=3, k=1), 3))      # 0.3
print(round(pass_at_k(n=10, c=3, k=5), 3))      # 0.917
print(round(token_f1("the cat sat", "a cat sat down"), 3))   # 0.571
```

Business link: an offline metric is a proxy. Always say how it connects to the online metric (A/B test) and to cost. See [A/B testing cheat sheet](#cheat-ab-testing), [Deployment and monitoring](#ai-deployment-monitoring). Docs: [sklearn model evaluation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html), [sklearn calibration](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html).

sections.body:
**How to use:** tables for definitions and defaults, the debugging table when training fails, PyTorch snippets for coding questions. Theory: [Neural networks](#ai-neural-networks), [Gradient descent](#ai-gradient-descent), [Embeddings](#ai-embeddings), [Attention and transformers](#ai-attention-transformer).

### Layers: shapes and parameter counts

| Layer | PyTorch | Input -> output shape | Parameters | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fully connected | `nn.Linear(d_in, d_out)` | `(B, d_in) -> (B, d_out)` | `d_in * d_out + d_out` | MLP, heads, projections |
| Embedding | `nn.Embedding(V, d)` | `(B, T)` ints -> `(B, T, d)` | `V * d` | tokens, IDs (users, items) |
| Conv 2D | `nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, k, stride, padding)` | `(B, c_in, H, W) -> (B, c_out, H', W')` | `k * k * c_in * c_out + c_out` | images, local patterns, weight sharing |
| Output size (conv / pool) | | `H' = floor((H + 2P - K) / S) + 1` | | `K=3, P=1, S=1` keeps size |
| Max / avg pooling | `nn.MaxPool2d(2)` | halves H and W | 0 | downsample, translation invariance |
| Global avg pool | `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)` | `(B, C, H, W) -> (B, C, 1, 1)` | 0 | before classifier head |
| RNN / LSTM / GRU | `nn.LSTM(d_in, h, batch_first=True)` | `(B, T, d_in) -> (B, T, h)` | LSTM: `4 (h d_in + h h + 2h)`; GRU: 3 gates | sequences (mostly replaced by transformers) |
| Multi-head attention | `nn.MultiheadAttention(d, heads, batch_first=True)` | `(B, T, d) -> (B, T, d)` | `4 d^2 + 4 d` | context mixing; cost O(T^2 d) |
| Transformer block | `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, heads, d_ff)` | `(B, T, d) -> (B, T, d)` | about `4 d^2 + 2 d d_ff` (`d_ff = 4d` -> `12 d^2`) | LLMs, encoders |
| Dropout | `nn.Dropout(p)` | same | 0 | regularization (off in eval) |
| Residual | `x + f(x)` | same | 0 | deep nets train (gradient highway) |

### Activations

| Name | Formula | Range | Use | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ReLU | `max(0, x)` | `[0, inf)` | default for hidden layers in CNN / MLP | dead neurons if always negative |
| Leaky ReLU | `x if x > 0 else 0.01 x` | all reals | avoid dead ReLU | |
| GELU | `x * Phi(x)` | about `[-0.17, inf)` | transformers (BERT, GPT) | smooth |
| SiLU / Swish | `x * sigmoid(x)` | about `[-0.28, inf)` | modern CNNs, LLMs (SwiGLU) | smooth |
| Sigmoid | `1 / (1 + exp(-x))` | `(0, 1)` | binary output, gates | saturates: vanishing gradient in hidden layers |
| Tanh | `(e^x - e^-x) / (e^x + e^-x)` | `(-1, 1)` | RNN, zero-centered | saturates |
| Softmax | `exp(z_i) / sum(exp(z_j))` | probabilities, sum 1 | multiclass output, attention | subtract max for stability |

### Losses (output layer -> loss)

| Task | Output | Loss | PyTorch | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| regression | linear | MSE / MAE / Huber | `nn.MSELoss()`, `nn.L1Loss()`, `nn.HuberLoss()` | Huber robust to outliers |
| binary | 1 logit | binary cross-entropy | `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=...)` | pass logits, not sigmoid output (stable) |
| multiclass (one label) | C logits | cross-entropy `-log softmax(z)[y]` | `nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)` | targets are class indices; no softmax before it |
| multilabel | C logits | BCE per label | `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()` | targets float 0 / 1 |
| imbalance / detection | logits | focal loss `-(1 - p_t)^gamma log p_t` | `torchvision.ops.sigmoid_focal_loss` | down-weights easy examples |
| distributions | log probs | KL divergence | `nn.KLDivLoss(reduction="batchmean")` | distillation; input is log prob |
| embeddings | vectors | contrastive / InfoNCE, triplet | `nn.TripletMarginLoss`, cross-entropy over similarity matrix | retrieval, two-tower |
| language model | V logits per token | next-token cross-entropy | `F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, V), y.view(-1))` | perplexity = `exp(loss)` |

### Optimizers

| Optimizer | Update (plain text) | Defaults | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| SGD | `w -= lr * g` | lr 0.01 to 0.1 | simple; noisy |
| SGD + momentum | `v = mu v + g; w -= lr v` | mu 0.9 | CNNs, good generalization |
| Nesterov | gradient at the look-ahead point | `nesterov=True` | slightly faster |
| AdaGrad | `w -= lr g / sqrt(sum g^2)` | | sparse features; lr decays too much |
| RMSProp | `s = rho s + (1 - rho) g^2; w -= lr g / sqrt(s + eps)` | rho 0.9 | RNNs |
| Adam | momentum `m` + RMS `v`, bias corrected: `w -= lr m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps)` | lr 1e-3, betas (0.9, 0.999) | default, fast convergence |
| AdamW | Adam + decoupled weight decay `w -= lr wd w` | lr 1e-4 to 3e-4 (transformers), wd 0.01 to 0.1 | transformers, LLM fine-tuning |

**Learning rate schedules**: warmup (linear, first 1 to 5% of steps, needed for transformers) then cosine decay; step decay; `ReduceLROnPlateau`; OneCycle. Batch size up by k -> try lr up by k (SGD) or sqrt(k) (Adam). LR is the most important hyperparameter.

### Regularization

| Method | How | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Weight decay / L2 | penalty `lambda * sum(w^2)`; AdamW `weight_decay` | do not decay biases and norm weights |
| Dropout | zero activations with prob p, scale by `1/(1-p)` in training | p 0.1 (transformers) to 0.5 (MLP); `model.eval()` turns it off |
| Early stopping | stop when validation loss stops improving (patience) | keep best checkpoint |
| Data augmentation | flips, crops, color, mixup, cutmix; text: back-translation | strongest for images |
| Label smoothing | target `1 - eps` for true class | better calibration, less overconfidence |
| Batch norm, smaller model | | implicit regularization |
| Gradient clipping | `clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0)` | stability (RNN, transformers), not really regularization |

### Initialization

| Scheme | Variance | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| Xavier / Glorot | `Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out)` | tanh, sigmoid, linear |
| He / Kaiming | `Var(w) = 2 / fan_in` | ReLU family |
| Small normal (std 0.02) | GPT style, residual projections scaled by `1 / sqrt(2 * layers)` | transformers |
| Zeros | biases only | all-equal weights = symmetric neurons that never differ |
| Pretrained | transfer learning | almost always best when available |

### Normalization

| Type | Normalizes over | Use | Train vs eval |
|---|---|---|---|
| BatchNorm | batch (per channel) | CNNs, large batches | uses running mean / var in eval: call `model.eval()` |
| LayerNorm | features of each example | transformers, RNNs, small batch | same in both |
| RMSNorm | features, no mean subtraction | modern LLMs (LLaMA) | same |
| GroupNorm | groups of channels | detection, tiny batches | same |
| Pre-norm vs post-norm | norm before sublayer (pre) is more stable for deep transformers | | |
| Input standardization | `(x - mean) / std` from training data | always for tabular / pixel input | |

### Debugging training

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| loss is NaN / inf | lr too high, log(0), division by 0, fp16 overflow | lower lr, use `BCEWithLogitsLoss` / `CrossEntropyLoss` (log-sum-exp inside), gradient clipping, bf16 / loss scaling, check inputs for NaN |
| loss does not go down at all | bug: wrong labels, forgot `zero_grad`, wrong loss input (softmax before CE), lr too low, frozen params | overfit one small batch first; check `requires_grad`; print grad norms |
| loss stuck at `log(C)` | predicts uniform; dead network | check data / labels shuffled together, init, lr |
| training loss down, validation up | overfitting | more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, smaller model |
| both high | underfitting | bigger model, train longer, higher lr, less regularization |
| loss oscillates | lr too high, batch too small | lower lr, warmup, larger batch |
| vanishing gradients | deep net with sigmoid / tanh | ReLU / GELU, residuals, normalization, He init |
| exploding gradients | RNNs, deep nets | gradient clipping, lower lr, normalization |
| validation metric differs between runs of eval | forgot `model.eval()` (dropout, BN still training) | `model.eval()` + `torch.no_grad()` |
| GPU out of memory | batch or sequence too long | smaller batch + gradient accumulation, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing |
| great validation, bad production | leakage, train / serve skew, shift | same preprocessing code, time-based split, monitor drift |

Checklist: (1) overfit 1 batch to near zero loss, (2) check the loss at init (CE about `log(C)`), (3) visualize inputs after preprocessing, (4) lr range test, (5) compare to a simple baseline.

### PyTorch: model + training loop
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

torch.manual_seed(0)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

X = torch.randn(1000, 20)
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).long()                       # 2 classes
train = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X[:800], y[:800]), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
val = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X[800:], y[800:]), batch_size=256)

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_hidden, n_classes, p=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_in, d_hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(p),
            nn.Linear(d_hidden, n_classes))               # logits, no softmax
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

model = MLP(20, 64, 2).to(device)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=10)

best, patience, bad = float("inf"), 3, 0
for epoch in range(10):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in train:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        opt.zero_grad()                                   # 1 reset
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)                     # 2 forward
        loss.backward()                                   # 3 backward
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()                                        # 4 update
    sched.step()

    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        vl, correct = 0.0, 0
        for xb, yb in val:
            xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
            logits = model(xb)
            vl += loss_fn(logits, yb).item() * len(yb)
            correct += (logits.argmax(1) == yb).sum().item()
    vl /= 200
    if vl < best:
        best, bad = vl, 0
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best.pt")         # keep best checkpoint
    else:
        bad += 1
        if bad >= patience:
            break
print(f"val loss {best:.3f} acc {correct / 200:.2f}")
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("best.pt"))
```

### PyTorch: overfit one batch, parameter count, shapes
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 3))
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad))   # 10*32+32 + 32*3+3 = 451

xb, yb = torch.randn(16, 10), torch.randint(0, 3, (16,))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
print(round(loss_fn(model(xb), yb).item(), 2), "vs log(3) =", round(torch.log(torch.tensor(3.0)).item(), 2))
for _ in range(300):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
print(loss.item() < 0.05)                                # True: the pipeline can learn

conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)
print(conv(torch.randn(8, 3, 32, 32)).shape)             # (8, 16, 16, 16): floor((32 + 2 - 3) / 2) + 1 = 16
print(sum(p.numel() for p in conv.parameters()))         # 3*3*3*16 + 16 = 448
emb = nn.Embedding(1000, 64)
print(emb(torch.randint(0, 1000, (4, 12))).shape)        # (4, 12, 64)
```

### PyTorch: attention from scratch, CNN, init, mixed precision
```python
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

def attention(q, k, v, causal=False):                     # (B, T, d)
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(q.size(-1))
    if causal:
        T = q.size(1)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))  # no peeking at the future
    return F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ v

q = k = v = torch.randn(2, 5, 8)
out = attention(q, k, v, causal=True)
ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
print(out.shape, torch.allclose(out, ref, atol=1e-5))    # (2, 5, 8) True

cnn = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),   # 28 -> 14
    nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),  # 14 -> 7
    nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32, 10))
print(cnn(torch.randn(4, 1, 28, 28)).shape)              # (4, 10)

for m in cnn.modules():                                  # He init for ReLU nets
    if isinstance(m, (nn.Conv2d, nn.Linear)):
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
        nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

# mixed precision step (bf16 autocast works on CPU and recent GPUs)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(cnn.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
x, y = torch.randn(4, 1, 28, 28), torch.randint(0, 10, (4,))
with torch.autocast(device_type="cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    loss = F.cross_entropy(cnn(x), y)
loss.backward()
opt.step()
opt.zero_grad()
print(round(loss.item(), 3) > 0)
```

### Transfer learning recipe
1. Load pretrained weights, replace the head (`model.fc = nn.Linear(in_features, n_classes)`).
2. Freeze the backbone (`p.requires_grad = False`), train the head with lr about 1e-3.
3. Unfreeze, fine-tune all with a small lr (1e-5 to 1e-4), discriminative lr per layer group if needed.
4. Same normalization as pretraining (e.g. ImageNet mean / std).

### Must-know answers
- **Why non-linear activations?** Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map.
- **Backprop** = chain rule applied from the loss backwards; cost about 2 times the forward pass.
- **Batch size**: larger = smoother gradients, faster per epoch on GPU, may generalize slightly worse; keep lr in sync.
- **Why residual connections?** Gradient flows directly through `x + f(x)`, so very deep nets train.
- **Why scale attention by `sqrt(d_k)`?** Dot products grow with dimension; large logits saturate softmax and kill gradients.
- **BatchNorm vs LayerNorm**: BN depends on batch statistics (bad for small batches and sequences); LN is per example.

Related: [LLM cheat sheet](#cheat-llm), [ML models](#cheat-ml-models), [Pretraining and decoding](#ai-pretraining-decoding). Docs: [PyTorch tutorials](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/), [torch.nn](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/nn.html), [Karpathy: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks](https://karpathy.github.io/2019/04/25/recipe/).

sections.title: LLMs
sections.summary: Token and cost math, decoding, prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, evals, safety and glossary.
sections.body:
**How to use:** back-of-envelope math first (cost, memory, latency), then the decision tables. Theory: [Attention and transformers](#ai-attention-transformer), [Pretraining and decoding](#ai-pretraining-decoding), [Fine-tuning and RLHF](#ai-fine-tuning-rlhf), [RAG](#ai-rag), [Agents](#ai-agents), [LLM evaluation](#ai-llm-evaluation), [Safety and cost](#ai-safety-cost).

### Tokens and cost math

| Rule of thumb | Value |
|---|---|
| English | 1 token approx 4 characters approx 0.75 words; 1,000 words approx 1,300 tokens |
| Korean, Persian, code | more tokens per word (often 1.5 to 3 times English) |
| Cost per request | `in_tokens * price_in / 1e6 + out_tokens * price_out / 1e6` (prices are per 1M tokens) |
| Output tokens | usually 3 to 5 times the price of input tokens; also slower (generated one by one) |
| Monthly cost | `requests per day * 30 * cost per request` |
| Latency | `time to first token (prefill, grows with prompt length) + out_tokens / tokens per second` |
| Prompt caching | repeated prefix (system prompt, documents) billed at a discount; put static content first |
| Batch APIs | about 50% cheaper for non-urgent jobs |

| Memory and compute | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|
| weights | `params * bytes` (fp32 4, fp16 / bf16 2, int8 1, int4 0.5) | 7B in bf16 = 14 GB; int4 = 3.5 GB |
| full fine-tune with Adam | about 16 bytes per param (weights, grads, 2 Adam states, fp32 master) + activations | 7B -> about 112 GB |
| LoRA params per adapted matrix | `r * (d_in + d_out)` | d 4096, r 8 -> 65,536 (0.4% of `4096^2`) |
| KV cache | `2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes` | 32 layers, 8 kv heads, 128 dim, 8k tokens, bf16 -> 1 GB per sequence |
| training compute | `FLOPs approx 6 * N * D` (N params, D tokens) | 7B x 2T tokens = 8.4e22 |
| inference compute | about `2 * N` FLOPs per token | |
| Chinchilla optimal | about 20 tokens per parameter | 7B -> 140B tokens (modern models train far longer) |
| attention cost | O(T^2 d) time, O(T^2) memory per head without FlashAttention | doubling context = 4 times attention cost |

```python
def cost_usd(in_tokens, out_tokens, price_in_per_m, price_out_per_m):
    return in_tokens * price_in_per_m / 1e6 + out_tokens * price_out_per_m / 1e6

# example prices (made up for the math): 3 per 1M input, 15 per 1M output
per_req = cost_usd(2_000, 500, 3.0, 15.0)
print(round(per_req, 4), round(per_req * 100_000 * 30))   # 0.0135 per request, 40500 per month at 100k/day

def kv_cache_gb(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per / 1e9

print(round(kv_cache_gb(32, 8, 128, 8192), 2))           # 1.07 GB
print(7e9 * 2 / 1e9, "GB bf16 weights for 7B")             # 14.0
print(4096 * 8 + 8 * 4096, "LoRA params for one 4096x4096 matrix, r=8")
```

### Decoding parameters

| Parameter | What it does | Typical value | Effect if too high / too low |
|---|---|---|---|
| greedy | always take the top token | temperature 0 | deterministic, can repeat |
| temperature T | divide logits by T before softmax | 0 to 0.3 facts, extraction, code; 0.7 to 1.0 creative | high: random, errors; low: repetitive |
| top-k | sample only from the k most likely tokens | 40 to 100 | fixed k ignores how peaked the distribution is |
| top-p (nucleus) | smallest set with cumulative prob >= p | 0.9 to 0.95 | adapts to confidence; tune T or p, not both |
| min-p | drop tokens with prob < min_p * top prob | 0.05 to 0.1 | good with high T |
| max tokens | output length cap | task dependent | cuts answers; controls cost |
| stop sequences | end generation at a string | e.g. a closing tag | |
| frequency / presence penalty | penalize tokens already used (by count / at all) | 0 to 1 | reduces repetition; too high hurts fluency |
| repetition penalty | divide logits of seen tokens | 1.1 to 1.3 | open models |
| beam search | keep b best partial sequences | b 4 | translation, short outputs; bland for chat |
| seed | reproducible sampling | fixed in evals | |
| structured output | JSON schema / constrained decoding | | guarantees parseable output |

```python
import numpy as np

def sample_next(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None, rng=np.random.default_rng(0)):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, dtype=float)
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(np.argmax(logits))                     # greedy
    z = logits / temperature
    if top_k is not None:
        kth = np.sort(z)[-top_k]
        z = np.where(z < kth, -np.inf, z)                 # keep k best
    p = np.exp(z - z.max())
    p /= p.sum()
    if top_p is not None:
        order = np.argsort(-p)
        cum = np.cumsum(p[order])
        keep = order[: np.searchsorted(cum, top_p) + 1]   # smallest set with mass >= top_p
        mask = np.zeros_like(p)
        mask[keep] = p[keep]
        p = mask / mask.sum()
    return int(rng.choice(len(p), p=p))

logits = [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]
print(sample_next(logits, temperature=0))                 # 0
print(sample_next(logits, top_k=2), sample_next(logits, top_p=0.7))
```

### Prompting patterns

| Pattern | How | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Clear instruction + role | task, audience, constraints, output format first | always |
| Few-shot | 2 to 5 input / output examples, diverse, same format | format or style is hard to describe |
| Chain of thought | "think step by step" or reasoning models; hide reasoning from end users if needed | math, logic, multi-step |
| Structured output | JSON schema, XML tags, delimiters around inputs | parsing by code |
| Decomposition / prompt chaining | split into steps, each a call | long complex tasks, easier debugging |
| Self-consistency | sample n answers, majority vote | reasoning accuracy, at n times cost |
| ReAct / tool use | reason, call tool, observe, repeat | needs fresh data or actions. See [Agents](#ai-agents) |
| Retrieval (RAG) | put relevant documents in the context with citations | private or fresh knowledge |
| Critique and revise | second pass checks the first against a rubric | quality-critical text |
| Grounding instruction | "answer only from the context; say I do not know otherwise" | reduce hallucination |
| Delimit untrusted input | mark user / document text as data, not instructions | prompt injection defense |

### RAG checklist

| Stage | Decisions | Common failure | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ingest | parse PDFs, HTML, tables; clean; metadata (source, date, access rights) | broken tables, boilerplate | good parsers, keep structure |
| Chunk | 200 to 800 tokens, 10 to 20% overlap, split on headings / sentences | answer split across chunks; chunk without context | semantic chunks, add title to each chunk, parent-document retrieval |
| Embed | embedding model fit to domain and language; same model for queries and docs | multilingual mismatch | multilingual model, fine-tune embeddings |
| Index | vector DB (FAISS, HNSW); metadata filters | stale index | incremental updates, versioning |
| Retrieve | top-k 5 to 20; hybrid BM25 + dense (reciprocal rank fusion) | exact terms missed (IDs, names) by dense search | hybrid search, query rewriting, HyDE |
| Rerank | cross-encoder on top 50 -> keep 5 | irrelevant chunks dilute context | reranker; fewer, better chunks |
| Generate | prompt with citations, "say I do not know" | hallucination, ignores context, lost in the middle | grounding prompt, put best chunks first / last, smaller context |
| Evaluate | retrieval: recall@k, MRR, context precision; generation: faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness | only end-to-end score, no diagnosis | evaluate retrieval and generation separately on a labeled set |
| Operate | latency, cost, access control, freshness, feedback logging | data leak across users | filter by permissions at retrieval |

```python
import numpy as np

docs = ["Refunds are allowed within 30 days of purchase.",
        "Shipping to Korea takes 5 to 7 business days.",
        "Premium members get free shipping on all orders."]
vocab = sorted({w.strip(".").lower() for d in docs for w in d.split()})

def embed(text):                                     # toy bag-of-words; use a real embedding model in practice
    words = [w.strip(".?").lower() for w in text.split()]
    v = np.array([words.count(t) for t in vocab], dtype=float)
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) + 1e-12)

D = np.stack([embed(d) for d in docs])
q = embed("How long does shipping to Korea take?")
scores = D @ q                                       # cosine similarity (vectors are normalized)
top = np.argsort(-scores)[:2]
context = "\n".join(f"[{i}] {docs[i]}" for i in top)
prompt = f"Answer only from the context. Cite sources.\nContext:\n{context}\nQuestion: How long does shipping to Korea take?"
print(top[0], prompt.splitlines()[2])                # 1 [1] Shipping to Korea takes 5 to 7 business days.
```

### Fine-tuning choices

| Option | Changes | Data needed | Use when | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prompt engineering + few-shot | nothing | 0 to 20 examples | first step, always | cheap; long prompts cost per call |
| RAG | context at inference | documents | knowledge is private, large, or changes often; need citations | retrieval quality is the bottleneck |
| SFT full fine-tune | all weights | 1k to 100k+ labeled pairs | new format, style, domain behavior; small model to replace a big one | expensive, catastrophic forgetting |
| LoRA / QLoRA (PEFT) | low-rank adapters (`W + B A`), base frozen; QLoRA = 4-bit base | 100s to 10k examples | most fine-tuning on limited GPUs; many adapters per base | slightly below full FT sometimes |
| Distillation | small student learns from big teacher outputs | teacher generations | cut latency and cost | check license, quality gap |
| Preference: RLHF (PPO) | reward model + RL with KL penalty to the SFT model | human preference pairs | align helpfulness / harmlessness | complex, unstable, reward hacking |
| Preference: DPO | direct loss on (chosen, rejected) pairs, no reward model | preference pairs | simpler alignment of tone, refusals | needs good pairs |
| Continued pretraining | next-token on domain corpus | millions+ tokens | new language or domain vocabulary | expensive |

Rule: **knowledge -> RAG; behavior / format / style -> fine-tune; both -> RAG + fine-tune.** Always start with prompting plus an eval set.

### Eval methods

| Level | Method | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Offline, reference based | exact match, F1, ROUGE, BLEU, pass@k, perplexity | see [ML metrics](#cheat-ml-metrics) |
| Offline, judge based | LLM-as-judge with rubric, pairwise preference, win rate | swap positions, calibrate against human labels, check agreement (kappa) |
| Human | expert rating, side by side | gold set, inter-rater agreement |
| RAG specific | context recall / precision, faithfulness, answer relevance | separate retrieval and generation errors |
| Safety | red teaming, jailbreak suite, toxicity, PII leakage, refusal and over-refusal rates | release gate |
| Regression suite | fixed golden set run on every prompt / model change | catches silent breakage |
| Online | A/B test: task success, thumbs up / down, retention, escalation to human, cost, latency | the final truth; see [A/B testing](#cheat-ab-testing) |
| Monitoring | drift in inputs, output length, refusal rate, judge scores on samples | see [Deployment and monitoring](#ai-deployment-monitoring) |

Eval set design: 100 to 500 real, diverse examples incl. edge cases and adversarial ones; stratify by intent; version it; no overlap with training or few-shot examples (contamination).

### Safety checklist

| Risk | Example | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt injection (direct and indirect) | "ignore previous instructions" in a user message or a retrieved web page | separate instructions from data, least-privilege tools, confirm actions with the user, output filtering |
| Jailbreak | role-play to get harmful content | safety-tuned model, input / output classifiers, red teaming |
| Hallucination | invented facts, citations | RAG with citations, "I do not know", verification step, lower temperature |
| PII and data leakage | model repeats personal data or other users' docs | PII redaction, access control at retrieval, no secrets in prompts, retention policy |
| Toxicity and bias | harmful or unfair outputs across groups | classifiers, fairness evals by group, human review |
| Unsafe tool actions | agent deletes data or sends money | allow-lists, sandbox, human approval for irreversible actions, rate limits |
| Cost and abuse | prompt flooding, long outputs | rate limits, max tokens, quotas, caching |
| Over-refusal | refuses harmless requests | measure false refusal rate, tune |
| Compliance | copyright, licenses, regional rules | logging, audit trail, policy review |

### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Token | unit of text the model reads (subword, from BPE / SentencePiece) |
| Context window | max tokens of input + output per call |
| Embedding | dense vector of meaning; similar meaning = high cosine similarity |
| Self-attention | each token mixes information from all (or earlier) tokens with weights `softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V` |
| Causal / decoder-only | GPT style: predicts the next token, attends only to the past |
| Encoder-only | BERT style: bidirectional, for classification and embeddings |
| Prefill / decode | process the prompt in parallel / generate tokens one by one |
| KV cache | stored keys and values of past tokens to avoid recomputation |
| Logits | raw scores before softmax |
| Perplexity | `exp(average negative log likelihood)`; lower is better |
| SFT | supervised fine-tuning on instruction / response pairs |
| RLHF | reinforcement learning from human feedback (reward model + PPO) |
| DPO | direct preference optimization, no reward model |
| LoRA / QLoRA | low-rank adapters; with a 4-bit quantized base |
| Quantization | lower precision weights (int8, int4) for memory and speed |
| Distillation | small model trained to imitate a large one |
| MoE | mixture of experts: router activates a few expert MLPs per token |
| RAG | retrieval-augmented generation |
| Hybrid search | sparse (BM25) + dense (embeddings) retrieval |
| Reranker | cross-encoder that rescores query-document pairs |
| Hallucination | fluent but false or unsupported output |
| Agent | LLM in a loop that plans, calls tools, observes results |
| Function / tool calling | model outputs a structured call that code executes |
| Grounding | tying answers to given sources |
| Temperature | randomness of sampling |
| Scaling law | loss falls as a power law in params, data, compute |
| Guardrails | input / output checks around the model |
| Contamination | test data seen in training; inflates scores |

Related: [Deep learning](#cheat-deep-learning), [Embeddings](#ai-embeddings), [Recommenders](#ai-recommenders), [Safety and cost](#ai-safety-cost). External: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), [Hugging Face LLM course](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course), [LoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685), [DPO paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290).

sections.title: Google Colab
sections.summary: Mount Drive, upload and download files, install packages, use a GPU, keyboard shortcuts and how not to lose work.
sections.body:
Code that starts with `!` runs in the shell; `%` is a notebook magic. Both only work inside Colab or Jupyter, not in a plain Python file.

### I want to ...

| I want to ... | Do this |
|---|---|
| open a notebook from Drive | double-click the `.ipynb` file in Drive -> Open with -> Google Colaboratory |
| open from GitHub | File -> Open notebook -> GitHub tab, paste the URL |
| use my data in Drive | mount Drive (code below); files are in `/content/drive/MyDrive/...` |
| upload a file from my computer | `files.upload()` or the folder icon on the left -> upload (lost when the runtime ends) |
| download a result | `files.download("out.csv")` |
| install a package | `%pip install -q packagename` |
| use a GPU | Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU -> Save |
| start clean | Runtime -> Restart session (variables cleared, files in `/content` kept) |
| start completely fresh | Runtime -> Disconnect and delete runtime (files in `/content` are deleted) |
| run everything | Runtime -> Run all (`Ctrl+F9`) |
| stop a cell that hangs | `Ctrl+M I` or the stop button on the cell |
| see variables | the `{x}` icon on the left |
| keep an API key out of the notebook | key icon on the left (Secrets), then `userdata.get("NAME")` |

### Mount Google Drive and find the data

```python
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount("/content/drive")            # click the link / allow access once per session
DATA = "/content/drive/MyDrive/exam_prep/data"
import os
print(os.listdir(DATA)[:10])
```

The notebooks use this loader. It works in Colab (searches Drive for `exam_prep/data`) and locally:
```python
import os, sys, glob

def find_data():
    if "google.colab" in sys.modules:
        from google.colab import drive
        drive.mount("/content/drive")
        hits = [p for depth in range(4)
                for p in glob.glob("/content/drive/MyDrive/" + "*/" * depth + "exam_prep/data")]
        if hits:
            return hits[0]
    for p in ("../data", "data", "exam_prep/data"):
        if os.path.isdir(p):
            return p
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
    return "data"

DATA = find_data()
```

If the mount fails or hangs: Runtime -> Restart session, run the cell again, or `drive.mount("/content/drive", force_remount=True)`.

### Upload and download files

```python
from google.colab import files
uploaded = files.upload()                # opens a file picker; returns {filename: bytes}
name = next(iter(uploaded))
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv(name)

df.to_csv("result.csv", index=False)
files.download("result.csv")             # browser download
```
Files in `/content` disappear when the runtime is recycled. Save anything you want to keep to Drive:
```python
df.to_csv("/content/drive/MyDrive/exam_prep/result.csv", index=False)
```

### Install packages

```python
%pip install -q lightgbm                 # installs into the running kernel
%pip install -q "scikit-learn==1.5.2"    # pin a version
import importlib.metadata as md
print(md.version("lightgbm"))
```
- Prefer `%pip` over `!pip`: it installs into the same environment as the notebook.
- If the import still fails, or an already imported package was upgraded: Runtime -> Restart session, then run the cells again (the install is kept until the runtime is deleted).
- Installs are lost when the runtime is recycled. Keep the `%pip` cell at the top of the notebook.
- Shell commands: `!ls -la`, `!head -5 file.csv`, `!wget URL`, `!unzip file.zip`, `!nvidia-smi`.

### GPU

```python
!nvidia-smi                              # shows the GPU and its memory
import torch
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
print(device, torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if device == "cuda" else "")
model = model.to(device)                 # move the model and every batch to the same device
x = x.to(device)
```
| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| `torch.cuda.is_available()` is False | change the runtime type to GPU, then rerun all cells |
| `CUDA out of memory` | smaller batch size, `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`, restart the session |
| "Cannot connect to GPU backend" | GPU quota used up; continue on CPU or try later |
| GPU idle during training | data loading is the bottleneck: `num_workers`, preload tensors |
| model and data on different devices | `RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device`: call `.to(device)` on both |

You do not need a GPU for the stats, SQL and classic ML notebooks. Use it only for neural network or embedding questions.

### Keyboard shortcuts (Windows; on Mac use Cmd instead of Ctrl)

| Action | Shortcut |
|---|---|
| run cell | `Ctrl+Enter` |
| run cell and go to the next | `Shift+Enter` |
| run cell and insert a new one below | `Alt+Enter` |
| run all | `Ctrl+F9` |
| run all cells before this one | `Ctrl+F8` |
| run this cell and all after | `Ctrl+F10` |
| interrupt | `Ctrl+M I` |
| restart session | `Ctrl+M .` |
| insert code cell above / below | `Ctrl+M A` / `Ctrl+M B` |
| delete cell | `Ctrl+M D` |
| undo cell deletion | `Ctrl+M Z` |
| convert to text (markdown) / to code | `Ctrl+M M` / `Ctrl+M Y` |
| move cell up / down | `Ctrl+M K` / `Ctrl+M J` |
| comment / uncomment line | `Ctrl+/` |
| command palette | `Ctrl+Shift+P` |
| show all shortcuts | `Ctrl+M H` |
| autocomplete | `Tab` (or wait after typing `.`) |
| save | `Ctrl+S` |

`Ctrl+M` then a letter means: press `Ctrl+M`, release, then press the letter.

### Save your work and avoid losing it

| Risk | Prevention |
|---|---|
| notebook opened from a link is not yours | File -> Save a copy in Drive (then work in the copy) |
| runtime disconnects after inactivity (about 90 minutes idle) or after the maximum session time (about 12 hours on the free tier; limits change) | variables are lost; rerun from the top. Keep the notebook runnable top to bottom |
| files written to `/content` vanish | write outputs to `/content/drive/MyDrive/...` |
| out-of-order execution hides bugs | before you trust a result: Runtime -> Restart session and run all |
| big outputs make the notebook slow to save | Edit -> Clear all outputs before saving |
| want a history | File -> Revision history; File -> Save a copy in GitHub |

### Useful magics and settings

```python
%time result = sum(range(10**6))         # line magic: times one statement
```
```python
%%timeit
sorted(range(10**5))
```
A cell magic (`%%`) must be the first line of its own cell.

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)     # show all columns
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 100)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:.4f}".format)
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)   # quieter output (fix real warnings first)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
```

| Magic | Use |
|---|---|
| `%time stmt` / `%%time` | run once and print the time |
| `%timeit stmt` / `%%timeit` | repeat and print a reliable timing |
| `%who` | list variables |
| `%load_ext autoreload` then `%autoreload 2` | reload your own `.py` files after editing them |
| `%cd /content/drive/MyDrive` | change the working folder |
| `%%writefile helper.py` | save the cell as a file |
| `%debug` | open the debugger after an exception |

### SQL inside Colab

The SQL notebooks use the built-in `sqlite3` module, nothing to install:
```python
import sqlite3, pandas as pd
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]}).to_sql("t", db, index=False)
pd.read_sql("SELECT SUM(x) AS s FROM t", db)
```

sections.summary: Per-round checklists: first words, clarifying questions, thinking aloud, timing, recovering when stuck, questions to ask.
sections.body:
### The day before and the hour before

| When | Check |
|---|---|
| day before | sleep is worth more than one more problem; light review of your mistake log and the cheat sheets only |
| day before | prepare 5 to 6 stories (STAR) and two "why this company / this team" answers |
| day before | test camera, microphone, internet, the coding platform (CoderPad, HackerRank, Google Docs) and screen sharing |
| 1 hour before | water, paper and pen, phone silent, notifications off, one browser window, quiet room |
| 30 min before | warm up: solve one easy problem out loud and write one SQL query with a window function |
| 5 min before | open the job description and your notes on the team; breathe slowly; smile when you join |

### The first two minutes of every round

1. Greet, say your name and one sentence about you (role, years, domain).
2. Listen to the question fully. Do not start coding or answering yet.
3. Restate the problem in your own words: "So the goal is ... given ... and the output is ... Is that right?"
4. Ask 2 to 4 clarifying questions (tables below).
5. Say your plan in one or two sentences before doing anything: "I will start with a simple approach, then improve it."

### Coding round (45 min, one or two problems)

| Minutes | What you do | What you say |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 5 | restate, clarify, write 1 to 2 examples with expected output | "Let me make sure I understand the input and output." |
| 5 to 10 | brute force + its complexity, then the better idea + its complexity | "The brute force is O(n^2). Using a hash map I can make it O(n). Shall I code that?" |
| 10 to 30 | code the agreed approach, clean names, small helper functions | narrate intent, not syntax: "Now I move the left pointer until the window is valid again." |
| 30 to 38 | dry-run your example line by line, then edge cases | "Let me trace the example. ... Now the empty input ..." |
| 38 to 42 | state time and space; mention one possible improvement | "Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n)." |
| 42 to 45 | your questions | |

Clarifying questions (coding):

| Ask about | Example question |
|---|---|
| input size | "How large can n be?" (this decides the target complexity, see [Big-O](#cheat-big-o)) |
| value range | "Can values be negative, zero, or very large? Floats?" |
| duplicates | "Can there be duplicates? Should the answer contain unique items?" |
| empty / tiny input | "What should I return for an empty list?" |
| sorted or not | "Is the input sorted?" |
| output format | "Indices or values? Any order? If several answers, return any one?" |
| modification | "May I modify the input in place?" |
| strings | "Only lowercase ASCII, or Unicode? Case-sensitive?" |
| graph / tree | "Can there be cycles? Is it connected? Is the tree balanced, is it a BST?" |

Edge cases to test before the examiner asks: empty, one element, all equal, already sorted, reverse sorted, negatives, duplicates, very large values, no valid answer.

### SQL round

| Step | What you do |
|---|---|
| 1 | ask for or write down the schema; confirm the grain of each table ("one row per order?") |
| 2 | define the metric exactly: numerator, denominator, time window, which users count |
| 3 | say the plan as CTE steps: "first per-user daily activity, then first day, then join" |
| 4 | write it step by step with readable CTE names |
| 5 | check: duplicates, NULLs, LEFT vs INNER, integer division, ties, time zones |
| 6 | sanity-check the output: row count, ranges, one example user by hand |

Clarifying questions (SQL): "Can a user have several rows per day?", "Are refunds or test accounts excluded?", "Which time zone are timestamps in?", "Should users with zero activity appear with 0?", "How should ties be ranked?", "Is the date range inclusive?". See [SQL exam approach](#sql-exam-approach).

### Statistics / A/B testing / product round

| Question type | Skeleton of a strong answer |
|---|---|
| design an A/B test | goal -> primary metric + guardrails -> unit of randomization -> hypothesis -> sample size from MDE, alpha, power -> duration (full weeks) -> checks (SRM, novelty) -> decision rule |
| analyze results | check SRM and data quality first -> effect + confidence interval -> practical vs statistical significance -> segments (with caution) -> recommendation |
| a metric dropped | clarify the metric and the size of the drop -> is it real (tracking, bug, seasonality)? -> internal vs external -> segment (platform, country, new vs old users, funnel step) -> hypotheses -> how to verify |
| should we launch? | trade-offs between metrics, long-term effects, cost, risk; a clear recommendation with conditions |
| probability puzzle | define events, write the formula, compute, sanity-check with an extreme case or a quick simulation |

Clarifying questions (stats / product): "What is the business goal?", "Who are the users and what is the unit (user, session, device)?", "What is the baseline rate and what lift matters?", "Are there network effects between users?", "What time frame?". Frameworks: [Case framework](#stats-case-framework), [A/B design](#stats-ab-design), [Metric drop](#stats-metric-drop), [Launch decisions](#stats-launch-decisions).

### Machine learning / AI round

| Step | Content |
|---|---|
| 1. frame | business goal -> ML task (classification, ranking, regression, generation) -> label definition |
| 2. data | sources, label quality, leakage risks, time-based split |
| 3. features / inputs | user, item, context, history; embeddings; for LLMs: prompt, retrieval context |
| 4. model | simple baseline first (logistic regression, popularity, GBDT), then the stronger model and why |
| 5. evaluation | offline metric that matches the goal (AUC, PR-AUC, NDCG, recall at k), then online A/B metric |
| 6. serving | latency and cost budget, batch vs real time, candidate generation + ranking |
| 7. monitoring | data drift, prediction drift, feedback loops, fairness, safety; retraining plan |

Clarifying questions (ML): "What is the cost of a false positive vs a false negative?", "How many items / users, and what latency?", "Do we have labels, and how delayed are they?", "Is this a new system or improving an existing one?". See [ML system design](#ai-ml-system-design) and [Classification metrics](#ai-classification-metrics).

### Behavioral round

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| format | STAR: Situation (1 to 2 sentences), Task, Action (most of the time, say "I"), Result (a number if possible) and what you learned |
| length | about 2 minutes per story; stop and let them ask follow-ups |
| stories to prepare | conflict with a colleague, failure or mistake, influence without authority, ambiguous project, tight deadline, impact you are proud of, a time data changed a decision |
| company values | read them; map each story to one value |

### Thinking aloud: useful sentences

| Situation | Sentence |
|---|---|
| starting | "Let me think about this for a moment and write down what I know." |
| choosing | "Two options: A is simpler, B is faster. Given n up to 10^5, I will go with B." |
| assumptions | "I will assume the input fits in memory; tell me if that is wrong." |
| while coding | "This loop keeps the invariant that everything left of i is processed." |
| checking | "Let me check this with the example before moving on." |
| finding your own bug | "This is off by one at the boundary; I will fix it here." |
| time pressure | "Given the time, I will finish the core logic first and handle the edge case after." |
| finishing | "I am done with the main solution. Would you like me to test more cases or optimize?" |

Silence longer than about 30 seconds feels long to the examiner. Say what you are checking, even if you do not know the answer yet.

### When you are stuck

1. Say it calmly: "I am stuck on how to avoid the second loop. Let me think out loud."
2. Go back to a small example and solve it by hand. Watch what you do.
3. Run through the signals: sorted input -> binary search or two pointers; "subarray / substring" -> sliding window or prefix sums; "top k" -> heap; "all combinations" -> backtracking; "min / max ways" -> DP; "connected / shortest" -> BFS or union-find. Use [Recognize the pattern](#algo-recognize) and [Pattern chooser](#cheat-algo-patterns).
4. Offer the brute force and code it if time is short. A working simple solution scores more than an unfinished clever one.
5. Ask a specific question, not "can you help?": "Would it help to sort first, or does the order matter?"
6. Take hints gracefully: "That makes sense, thank you", then use the hint immediately.
7. Made a mistake? Fix it openly. Examiners score how you debug, not only if you are right first time.

### Time management

| Round | Rule |
|---|---|
| coding | no code before an agreed approach; but start coding by minute 12 at the latest |
| two problems in one round | about 20 minutes each; do not polish the first while the second waits |
| SQL with several parts | answer each part fully before the next; reuse CTEs |
| stats / case | structure first (30 seconds), then depth; check the time halfway |
| any round | if you spend more than 5 minutes on one detail, state the assumption and move on |

### Questions to ask the examiner

| About | Question |
|---|---|
| the work | "What does a typical week look like for a data scientist on this team?" |
| impact | "Can you share a recent analysis or model that changed a product decision?" |
| team | "How do data scientists work with engineers and product managers here?" |
| tools | "What does the data stack look like, and how do experiments get run and reviewed?" |
| success | "What would success in the first six months look like for this role?" |
| challenges | "What is the hardest open problem the team is working on now?" |
| growth | "How do people on the team learn and grow? Is there mentoring?" |
| the examiner | "What do you enjoy most about working here?" |

Avoid asking about salary or benefits in technical rounds (keep that for the recruiter), and avoid questions answered on the first page of the company website.

### Last-minute checklist (print this)

- Restate, clarify, examples, plan, then code.
- Brute force first, with its complexity, then optimize.
- Talk while you work; no long silences.
- Test with your example and the edge cases; state time and space.
- SQL: grain, NULLs, duplicates, LEFT vs INNER, integer division, ties.
- A/B: metric, unit, power, SRM, guardrails, decision.
- ML: baseline, metric that matches the goal, leakage, monitoring.
- Stuck: small example, signals, brute force, specific question.
- End every round with one good question and a thank you.
